symptoms: Holes in leaves, buds, and flowers Larvae boring into fruits or pods Damaged cotton bolls and young fruits Presence of frass (insect excrement) around feeding sites Premature dropping of flowers or fruits
description: The larval stage of the cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) is the most destructive phase of this pest. The caterpillars feed aggressively on leaves, buds, flowers, fruits, and seeds of many crops. Larvae vary in color from green, brown, pink, or black and usually have longitudinal stripes along the body. Because they feed directly on reproductive plant structures, they can cause significant yield losses in crops such as cotton, tomato, maize, and chickpea.
management: monitoring: Inspect plants regularly for eggs and young larvae Use pheromone traps to monitor adult moth populations Check buds, flowers, and fruits for feeding damage cultural_control: Crop rotation with non-host crops Removal of weeds and crop residues Deep ploughing after harvest to destroy pupae Planting trap crops such as sunflower or marigold mechanical_control: Handpicking and destroying larvae Removing infested fruits and plant parts Using pheromone and light traps to monitor populations biological_control: microorganisms: Helicoverpa nucleopolyhedrovirus (HaNPV) Baculovirus species targeting larvae Isaria fumosorosea macroorganisms: Trichogramma pretiosum (egg parasitoid wasp) Habrobracon hebetor (larval parasitoid) chemical_control: note: Chemical insecticides should be used only when pest populations exceed economic thresholds and as part of an Integrated Pest Management strategy. active_ingredients: Spinosad Emamectin benzoate Indoxacarb Lambda-cyhalothrin Chlorantraniliprole
